candidates.attacker_control: An attacker who can influence the XML/JSON text passed to XStream.fromXML/unmarshal (or a Java object stream read via XStream.createObjectInputStream) supplies the element/attribute type names. Because the <class>/resolves-to attributes are resolved against AnyTypePermission.ANY and the blacklist is inert, the attacker chooses arbitrary class names, including java.beans.EventHandler, java.lang.ProcessBuilder and arbitrary interface names for a dynamic proxy.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that no other component rejects these types in the default configuration: SecurityMapper returns the type whenever AnyTypePermission.ANY is present (SecurityMapper.java:70-78) and is the only permission by default; searched xstream/src/java for 'EventHandler', 'java.beans' and 'javax.crypto' - the InternalBlackList at XStream.java:2537-2546 is the only in-source blocker (JavaClassConverter only yields Class objects); verified the void/Void branch of InternalBlackList is unconditional and still works, so the CVE-2017-7957 DoS protection (PrimitiveTypePermission, security/PrimitiveTypePermission.java:24-27) is not affected; verified the blacklist does reject marshalling of these types while insecureWarning is still true, so the defect is specific to the unmarshal path; considered that users who explicitly initialize a whitelist (setupDefaultSecurity/denyTypes) before deserializing are protected by SecurityMapper regardless - the flaw applies to the default/drop-in configuration that the blacklist and FAQ text explicitly describe. No runtime execution or upstream history was available, so the mapping to a specific CVE/fix commit is inference, not confirmation.
candidates.impact: Security-control bypass leading to deserialization of types the library documents as not handled by default. This re-enables the documented arbitrary-command-execution scenario (EventHandler + dyn. proxy + ProcessBuilder.start()) and the other revoked types (*$LazyIterator, javax.crypto.*) for any application running default-configured XStream on untrusted data, i.e., remote code execution in the documented CVE-2013-7285 setting. Additionally, applications that follow the library's guidance by calling XStream.setupDefaultSecurity() after a first unmarshal receive no protection without any error being raised.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses a default-configured XStream instance (new XStream(); the drop-in 1.4.x mode in which the security framework was not explicitly initialized) and deserializes attacker-influenced input. For the documented end-to-end RCE scenario the application relies on the documented default contract that EventHandler is not handled, and the payload's proxy method is later invoked by application code (see xstream-distribution/src/content/CVE-2013-7285.html:35-54); the dangerous objects are nonetheless instantiated and populated during deserialization itself.
candidates.root_cause: State-machine ordering defect in XStream's implicit blacklist. During construction, setupSecurity() sets the permission list to AnyTypePermission.ANY and marks the instance insecure (XStream.java:693-700). The internal blacklist converter is registered at PRIORITY_LOW (XStream.java:964), but its canConvert() only rejects the dangerous types while the insecureWarning flag is still true (XStream.java:2541-2545). However, unmarshal(reader, root, dataHolder) sets insecureWarning = false *before* calling the marshalling strategy (XStream.java:1482-1485), and all converter lookups happen inside that strategy (TreeUnmarshaller.start -> convertAnother -> DefaultConverterLookup.lookupConverterForType, TreeUnmarshaller.java:131-141, DefaultConverterLookup.java:64-86). Consequently InternalBlackList.canConvert() always returns false for every element of every fromXML/unmarshal/createObjectInputStream call, and the ReflectionConverter (registered PRIORITY_VERY_LOW, XStream.java:958-959, canConvert true for any non-null type, ReflectionConverter.java:37-39) instantiates the blacklisted types instead. The SecurityMapper adds no further restriction because the default permission is AnyTypePermission.ANY (SecurityMapper.java:70-78).
candidates.title: Implicit security blacklist is never applied during unmarshalling (insecureWarning cleared before converter lookup), so default-configured XStream handles known RCE gadget types such as java.beans.EventHandler
candidates.trace: 1) new XStream() -> setupMappers(), setupSecurity() (XStream.java:588-589) -> addPermission(AnyTypePermission.ANY); insecureWarning = true (XStream.java:698-699). 2) fromXML(xml) -> unmarshal(reader, null, null) -> unmarshal(reader, root, dataHolder): the guard at XStream.java:1482-1485 flips insecureWarning to false and then calls marshallingStrategy.unmarshal(...). 3) TreeUnmarshaller.start() reads the root class via HierarchicalStreams.readClassType (mapper.realClass -> SecurityMapper with AnyTypePermission.ANY, allowed) and calls convertAnother; for each nested element the type from the class attribute is likewise resolved through the mapper and the converter is chosen by DefaultConverterLookup.lookupConverterForType. 4) At that point InternalBlackList.canConvert(type) evaluates 'insecureWarning && ...' with insecureWarning already false, so it returns false for java.beans.EventHandler; the chain falls through to ReflectionConverter, which allocates and populates the EventHandler (target, action fields) and to DynamicProxyConverter, which builds the proxy and installs the handler (DynamicProxyConverter.java:121-134). 5) The result is the object graph of the well-known CVE-2013-7285 RCE payload ('<dynamic-proxy><interface>...</interface><handler class="java.beans.EventHandler"><target class="java.lang.ProcessBuilder"><command>...</command></target><action>start</action></handler></dynamic-proxy>', documented verbatim in xstream-distribution/src/content/CVE-2013-7285.html:35-47), instead of the documented 'Security alert. Unmarshalling rejected.' ConversionException (XStream.java:2553-2555). 6) Same root cause, second effect: setupDefaultSecurity(xstream) is guarded by 'if (xstream.insecureWarning)' (XStream.java:713-715); after any earlier unmarshal the flag is already false, so the documented whitelist helper silently installs nothing and the ANY permission remains in force.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Could not consult git history, upstream patches or CVE data in this run, so the exact upstream fix (make the blacklist unconditional vs. defer the insecureWarning reset) is inferred. Whether a fully automatic trigger exists at deserialization time for every gadget type on every classpath was not verified; the repository's own documentation states that the EventHandler payload fires when application code next invokes a method on the deserialized proxy, which is the impact scenario assumed here. Classpath-dependent third-party gadgets were not enumerated.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data / security-control bypass (CWE-502, CWE-693)

coverage_summary: Scope: 763 model-visible files (695 parsed Java files) of the XStream repository at 1.4.11-SNAPSHOT. I inspected the whole core deserialization path (XStream.java constructors, setupSecurity/setupConverters, marshal/unmarshal, InternalBlackList; TreeUnmarshaller; DefaultConverterLookup; abstract marshalling strategies), the full com.thoughtworks.xstream.security package, the mapper chain (SecurityMapper, MapperWrapper delegation optimization), representative converters (ReflectionConverter, DynamicProxyConverter, TreeSet/TreeMap, JavaClass/JavaField/JavaMethod, Path/File/URL, JSON writer escaping) and the XML drivers' entity handling, plus the security-relevant site content (security.html, faq.html, CVE-2013-7285.html, CVE-2016-3674.html, CVE-2017-7957.html, changes.html). The P1 relation index was used only for navigation (facts are name-based hints; control_flow and data_flow are 'not_implemented', semantic_resolution 'not_implemented'), and every traced edge was re-verified in source text. Not exhaustively reviewed: xstream-hibernate, xstream-benchmark, the majority of unit tests, the annotation machinery, and many individual converters.
limitations: No execution, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were run; the blacklist bypass is demonstrated by source reasoning only.
The relation index is partial (13 omitted files, 2 parse errors) and offers no control-flow/data-flow proof, so the trace is manual.
One source-scope file is excluded for a sensitive name/path and was not available for review; I also did not verify which specific files the index omitted.

Git history, upstream patches and CVE metadata are outside this run, so the association with a specific upstream fix/CVE (e.g. the 2019 XStream blacklist regression) is inference from version, documentation and code state.

Third-party gadget availability on the deployment classpath and any automatic deserialization-time trigger were not verified; the impact scenario follows the repository's own CVE-2013-7285 documentation.

rejected_leads.reason: External-entity processing is explicitly disabled in DomDriver, Dom4JDriver, JDomDriver, JDom2Driver and StaxDriver (disallow-doctype-decl / IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false), and the residual XOM/old-StAX weakness is a documented upstream limitation (CVE-2016-3674.html:36-44), not a new defect.

rejected_leads.lead: Blacklist incompleteness: java.lang.ProcessBuilder and other gadget types are absent from InternalBlackList (XStream.java:2543-2545)
rejected_leads.reason: Considered as a separate candidate but kept inside the primary finding: because the list is inert during unmarshalling, adding entries cannot change behavior; incompleteness alone is a documented 'false sense of security' limitation (security.html:68-70) and is not reported as an independent root cause.

Documented and intentional for the 1.4.x drop-in series (security.html:93-98, FAQ:709-725) with whitelist guidance; reporting it separately would duplicate the primary finding's configuration context.

rejected_leads.lead: JavaClassConverter resolves class names through a plain DefaultMapper that lacks SecurityMapper (XStream.java:1003, JavaClassConverter.java:38-40, 67-73), potentially bypassing a configured whitelist when java.lang.Class is allowed
rejected_leads.reason: Produces Class objects rather than instantiated objects; no concrete sink or default-configuration impact could be established from source alone, so it is left as an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Thread-unsafe DefaultConverterLookup type cache (GHI:#2 'Unneeded contention', recent change)
rejected_leads.reason: Correctness/performance change, no attacker-controlled security impact demonstrated.

summary: XStream 1.4.11-SNAPSHOT (pom.xml:17; changes.html "Upcoming 1.4.x maintenance release"). The strongest source-evidenced issue is a logic flaw in the default (uninitialized) security state: the internal blacklist of known deserialization gadgets (`java.beans.EventHandler`, `*$LazyIterator`, `javax.crypto.*`) is registered but can never trigger during unmarshalling, because `XStream.unmarshal()` clears `insecureWarning` before any converter lookup while `InternalBlackList.canConvert()` requires that flag to be true. The repository's own documentation promises the opposite ("Since XStream version 1.4.7 it does no longer handle an EventHandler automatically", faq.html:699-706; "XStream itself sets up a black list by default, i.e. it blocks all currently known critical classes of the Java runtime", security.html:93-98). A default-configured XStream therefore instantiates the exact gadget class used by the documented CVE-2013-7285 remote-command-execution payload. A secondary effect of the same premature reset is that the documented `XStream.setupDefaultSecurity()` helper silently becomes a no-op after the first unmarshal.
